## merge vs rebase

**merge** — join two branches, keep full history. Creates merge commit.

```
A---B---C  main
     \
      D---E  feature
           \
            M  ← merge commit (has 2 parents)
```

**rebase** — replay feature commits on top of target. Linear history, no merge commit.

```
A---B---C  main
             \
              D'--E'  ← replayed commits (new hashes)
```

---

## when use each

**merge when:**
- shared/public branch (never rewrite pushed commits)
- want preserve exact history + context
- merging main → long-lived feature (safe catch-up)
- team unfamiliar with rebase

**rebase when:**
- local cleanup before PR
- want linear, readable history
- squashing noise commits
- updating feature off latest main (before push)

---

## tradeoffs

| | merge | rebase |
|---|---|---|
| history | true, messy | clean, rewritten |
| conflicts | once | per replayed commit |
| safety | always safe | dangerous on public branches |
| bisect/blame | harder | easier |
| context | preserves "when" | loses "when" |

---

## golden rule

> **Never rebase commits already pushed to shared branch.**

Rebase rewrites hashes. Others have old hashes. Chaos follows.

---

## common patterns

```bash
# update feature off main (local only)
git checkout feature
git rebase main

# clean up before PR (squash noise)
git rebase -i HEAD~4

# merge feature → main (preserve context)
git checkout main
git merge --no-ff feature
```

`--no-ff` force merge commit even if fast-forward possible. Good for explicit "feature landed here" marker in history.
